segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole five years in seven sits looked back at year two, the texts under the stories. Today, year three, and whose great story walks in: the Mahabharata's, in one scene.
screen: `THE TEXTS UNDER THE STORIES.` · `TODAY: YEAR THREE.`

segments.voice: A pop quiz is bad enough on a good day. Here's a worse one. Four brothers are lying still at the edge of a clear lake: Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, Bhima. The eldest, Yudhishthira, has come out of the forest looking for them, and he's found them. He's grieving, and he's so thirsty he kneels to drink. Then a voice from the water: don't. Your brothers drank before answering me. Answer my questions first. So what does he do?
screen: `A POP QUIZ, ON A BAD DAY.` → `FOUR BROTHERS BY A LAKE.` → `ANSWER ME BEFORE YOU DRINK.`

segments.voice: He answers. The voice belongs to a yaksha, a spirit of the place, and its questions come fast. What is quicker than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than the grass? Thoughts. Then the one people still repeat. What is the greatest wonder? Yudhishthira says: day after day, creatures go to the realm of death, and those who remain act as if they will live forever. What could be more wonderful than that? The yaksha is satisfied, and offers him one brother back. Only one. Bhima is the strong one; Arjuna is the archer. Either would make sense with a war ahead. Yudhishthira asks for Nakula. My father had two wives, he says, Kunti and Madri. I'm Kunti's son, and I'm alive. Let Madri have a living son too. Then the yaksha shows who he is: Dharma, Yudhishthira's own father, and he gives back all four. Year three of this path was the great story: the Mahabharata told as a serial, then Krishna's childhood, the saints, the modern teachers. If one sit had to hold that year, this scene comes close: a question about death asked by a lake, and an answer that chooses fairness over strength.
screen: `QUICKER THAN WIND: THE MIND.` · `THE GREATEST WONDER.` · `ONE BROTHER BACK: NAKULA.` · `THE VOICE WAS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Say softly, out loud, the name of one person you'd want to hear from you while there's time. Then say the one plain sentence you'd tell them: a thank-you, an apology, I'm glad you're here. Let it hang in the air for a few breaths; it doesn't have to go anywhere yet.
The whole five years in seven sits: the path, looked back on one scene at a time. Year three's scene is a lake, a voice, and the greatest wonder.

howItsDone: The yaksha's questions are retold in Hindu homes, storytelling and recitations of the Mahabharata's forest book, and readers of the epic often quote the 'greatest wonder' answer.

chat.meaning: The greatest wonder, Yudhishthira says, is that people see endings all around and act as if theirs won't come. Saying the real thing answers it.

Yudhishthira.meaning: eldest of the five Pandava brothers, son of Dharma

yaksha.meaning: a spirit of a place; here, the voice at the lake

Nakula.meaning: one of the five brothers, a son of Madri

Madri.meaning: the second wife of the brothers' father, mother of Nakula and Sahadeva

Dharma.meaning: the god of right order, Yudhishthira's father

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana (Aranyaka) Parva, the Yaksha Prashna (Ganguli's sections 311–313): the brothers drink and fall; the voice demands answers first; quicker than the wind, the mind; more numerous than grass, thoughts; the greatest wonder; one brother may live; Yudhishthira chooses Nakula for Madri's sake; the yaksha is Dharma and restores all four

notes: Block 'the whole five years in seven sits', day 3 of 4 (1777–1780), following the plan in 1777's note: 1777 year one, 1778 year two, 1779 year three, 1780 years four and five. The review answers 1778's 'tomorrow' (year three: whose great story walks in next?) with the Mahabharata's.

Story shape: the hook drops into the scene at the lake; the teach answers its cliffhanger. Surprising fact: Yudhishthira picks Nakula, not a stronger brother, so both of his father's wives have a living son.

Please check the paraphrase against Ganguli (Vana Parva 311–313): the order of the brothers' deaths, 'quicker than the wind / the mind', 'more numerous than grass / thoughts', the greatest-wonder answer, and the Kunti/Madri reasoning. The text's own superlative ('what is the most wonderful') is kept. The epic gives many more questions; the script says only that they come fast and gives no count.

The yaksha first appears as a crane in the epic; the script leaves that detail out. The Yaksha Prashna was probably taught in year three's Mahabharata serial; this day uses it only as the year's summary scene.
Hard scene, one gentle line for parents: the brothers lie dead by the lake before they are restored; the script keeps it brief ('lying still').
Practice kind: say it out loud (1778 was write by hand).
